title: Dairy calf and heifer rearing, feeding and health care

lessons.title: How a calf's digestion develops
lessons.html:
A calf is not a small cow

An adult cow is a ruminant: her rumen, a large fermentation chamber, digests grass and roughage with the help of microbes. A newborn calf's rumen is small and does not work yet. For the first weeks the calf lives like a simple-stomached animal on milk.

The oesophageal groove

When a calf sucks milk from a teat or bucket, a fold called the oesophageal groove closes and sends the milk straight to the abomasum (true stomach), bypassing the rumen. This is why milk should be fed at a consistent temperature and in a calm setting, so the groove closes properly.

Developing the rumen

The rumen grows and starts working when the calf eats solid feed. Three things drive rumen development:

  • Calf starter: palatable concentrate. Its fermentation produces acids that make the rumen wall grow its absorbing papillae.
  • Water: free access from the first days. Microbes need water; milk does not count as water because it bypasses the rumen.
  • Some fibre: small amounts of good hay or straw help rumen muscle and keep the pH stable.

Colostrum and immunity

Calves are born with very little immunity because antibodies do not cross the placenta in cattle. They depend on antibodies in colostrum, which the gut can absorb only for a short time after birth; absorption falls quickly over the first day. Failure of passive transfer, when a calf gets too little or poor colostrum too late, leads to more scours, pneumonia and deaths.

Good colostrum management means: feed early, feed enough, feed good quality (tested with a colostrometer or Brix refractometer) and feed it clean. Follow your farm's protocol and your vet's advice on volumes.

lessons.title: Feeding programmes from birth to calving
lessons.html:
Milk feeding phase

After colostrum and transition milk, calves are fed whole milk or milk replacer until weaning.

OptionAdvantagesPoints to watch
Whole milkNatural, highly digestibleUses saleable milk; waste milk with residues raises resistance concerns
Milk replacerConsistent, can be cheaper per calfMust be mixed exactly as per label; quality varies between products

Feeding systems include buckets, teat buckets, and automatic calf feeders. Consistency in time, amount, concentration and temperature is more important than the system.

Weaning

Weaning should depend on starter intake, not only age. A calf that eats enough starter has a working rumen and will not lose condition when milk stops. Reduce milk gradually over a week or more to encourage starter intake. Avoid other stresses, such as dehorning or moving, at weaning.

Post-weaning heifers

Heifers should grow steadily to reach breeding weight, commonly a target percentage of the mature cow weight set by the farm, at the planned age. Key points:

  • Feed quality roughage plus concentrate and minerals to meet growth targets.
  • Avoid overfeeding energy before puberty, which can lay down fat in the udder tissue.
  • Group by size to reduce bullying.
  • Weigh regularly and compare with targets for the breed.

In-calf heifers

Keep in-calf heifers growing; they still need to reach mature size. Introduce them to the parlour and the milking herd before calving to reduce stress. Close-up heifers get the transition ration with the cows or a similar one.

A heifer calving at the right age and size has fewer calving problems, gives more milk and lasts longer in the herd. Rearing is an investment; every month a heifer is late to calve costs the farm money.

lessons.title: Calf and heifer health
lessons.html:
Main health problems

Neonatal scours

Diarrhoea in young calves is caused by infections such as E. coli, rotavirus, coronavirus, cryptosporidium and salmonella, and by nutritional problems such as wrongly mixed replacer. The main danger is dehydration and loss of salts. Treatment is fluid and electrolyte replacement as advised by the vet; antibiotics only when the vet prescribes them. Prevention: colostrum, hygiene, clean dry bedding, and vaccination of dams where the vet recommends.

Pneumonia

Respiratory disease is linked to poor ventilation, draughts, damp, crowding, mixing ages and low immunity. Signs include coughing, nasal discharge, fast breathing and fever. Early detection and vet treatment reduce lung damage that can affect lifetime yield.

Navel infections

Dip navels at birth and keep calving areas clean. Swollen, hot navels need vet attention.

Parasites and tick-borne disease

Heifers on pasture face worms, coccidiosis, ticks and the diseases ticks carry, such as redwater, gallsickness and heartwater in certain areas. The vet will advise on deworming, tick control and vaccination for your area. Follow product labels.

Herd health plan for young stock

  • Vaccinations as the vet prescribes; brucellosis vaccination of heifer calves is controlled under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.
  • Disbudding with pain relief by a trained person.
  • Removal of extra teats when young, by a trained person.
  • Regular weighing and health checks.

Hygiene and housing

Clean, dry, well-ventilated housing without draughts at calf level is the best medicine. Clean feeding equipment after every feed. Feed sick calves last and keep a separate sick pen.

Welfare

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 forbids unnecessary suffering. Bull calves must receive colostrum, feed and care equal to heifers until they leave the farm, and transport must be humane.

Key points

  • The rumen develops with starter, water and some fibre.
  • Colostrum early, enough, good and clean prevents most early losses.
  • Wean on starter intake, not age alone.
  • Grow heifers steadily to target weight and age.
  • Prevent scours and pneumonia with colostrum, hygiene and good housing.
